summary: Updates the RTP payload formats for the EVRC codec family from RFC 3558. It adds header-free and interleaved or bundled formats for EVRC-B, and a compact bundled format for EVRC and EVRC-B.

plainLanguage.summary: EVRC is a speech codec for mobile networks, and EVRC-B is a newer version of it. This RFC adds media types so that both can be sent over RTP, including a compact way to pack several speech frames into one packet. It also adds the settings that let a sender stop transmitting during silence.

questions: what is the compact bundled format
what is dtx silence suppression in rtp
subtitle: New ways to send EVRC and EVRC-B speech over RTP, and the parameters that turn on silence suppression.

tldr.problem: The RTP payload formats for the EVRC speech codec were defined before the EVRC-B codec existed, and they carried a table of contents in every packet that cost bandwidth on exactly the slow links where voice matters most.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers new media types for EVRC-B and for a compact bundled format that puts several frames of the same rate in one packet without a table of contents, and it adds four optional parameters that negotiate silence suppression.
tldr.outcome: Six EVRC and EVRC-B media types are defined, with backward compatibility to RFC 3558 kept by making the silence suppression parameters receiver options that older implementations simply ignore.

today: RFC 4788 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 5188, which covers the EVRC-WB codec and revises the EVRC-B media subtypes. The document itself updated RFC 3558, which remains the base specification for the EVRC payload formats, and the silence suppression parameters were added as receiver options so that older implementations keep working unchanged.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines support for the header-free and interleaved/bundled packet formats for the EVRC-B codec, a new compact bundled format for the EVRC and EVRC-B codecs, and discontinuous transmission support for EVRC and EVRC-B-encoded speech transported via RTP. Voice over IP applications operating over low bandwidth dial-up and wireless networks require such EVRC RTP payload capabilities for efficient use of the bandwidth.

The document is an update to the RTP payload formats defined in RFC 3558. It works in three directions: it makes the newer EVRC-B codec usable over RTP with the formats that already existed, it adds a compact bundled format that saves the overhead of a table of contents, and it defines the optional parameters that let a session agree to suppress silence.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things are added here. The EVRC-B codec can now be sent over RTP at all. There is a leaner way to pack speech into packets. And there is a way for the two ends to agree to stop sending during silence.

sections.title: The EVRC-B Codec
sections.content:
EVRC-B is an extension to EVRC developed in the Third Generation Partnership Project 2. It compresses each 20 milliseconds of 8000 Hz, 16-bit sampled speech input into output frames of one of four different sizes: Rate 1 at 171 bits, Rate 1/2 at 80 bits, Rate 1/4 at 40 bits, or Rate 1/8 at 16 bits. In addition there are two zero-bit codec frame types, null frames and erasure frames, similar to EVRC. One significant enhancement in EVRC-B is the use of 1/4-rate frames that were not used in EVRC, which provides lower average data rates compared to EVRC for a given voice quality.

Since speech frames encoded by EVRC-B are different from those encoded by EVRC, the two codecs do not interoperate with each other. At the initiation of an RTP session the sender and receiver need to indicate, for example by using MIME subtypes separate from those of EVRC, that EVRC-B is to be used for the ensuing session.
sections.plainLanguage: EVRC-B encodes 20 milliseconds of speech at a time, at 8000 samples per second. It can pick one of four frame sizes, from 171 bits down to 16 bits, and it adds a quarter-rate frame that plain EVRC does not have, which is what makes it cheaper.

sections.title: Choosing a Packet Format
sections.content:
The interleaved/bundled packet format defined in RFC 3558 allows bundling of multiple speech frames of different rates in a single RTP packet, sending mode change requests, and interleaving. To support these functions a Table of Contents is used in each RTP packet, in addition to the standard RTP header. The size of the Table of Contents varies depending on the number of EVRC frames carried in the packet.

The header-free packet format defined in RFC 3558 is more compact and optimized for use over wireless links. It eliminates the need for a Table of Contents by requiring that each RTP packet contain only one speech frame of any allowable rate, so bundling is not allowed. Interleaving and mode change requests are not supported in the header-free format.

The compact bundled format described in this document presents an alternative to the header-free format. It allows bundling of multiple EVRC or EVRC-B frames without the addition of extra headers, as would be the case in the interleaved/bundled format. However, in order to use it, only one EVRC or EVRC-B rate, full rate or half rate, can be used in the session. As with the header-free format, interleaving and mode change requests are not supported in the compact bundled format.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to pack speech into RTP packets. The old interleaved format is flexible but adds a table of contents to every packet. The header-free format drops the table but allows only one frame per packet. The new compact format bundles frames but without the table, at the cost of using a single rate for the whole session.

sections.title: The Compact Bundled Packet
sections.content:
A packet in the compact bundled format consists of an RTP header followed by a sequence of one or more consecutive EVRC or EVRC-B codec data frames of the same rate. The codec data frames must be generated from the output of the codec following the procedure described in section 5.2 of RFC 3558, and all must be of the same rate and size.

As mentioned earlier, in order to use the compact bundled format all the EVRC or EVRC-B data frames in the session must be of the same rate, and this packet format may carry only full or half-rate frames. For a session that uses the compact bundled format, the rate for the session can be determined during the session setup signalling, for example via Session Description Protocol exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: The compact packet is simple: an ordinary RTP header, then a row of speech frames that are all the same size. The rate is agreed during the session setup.

sections.title: Storage Format for EVRC-B
sections.content:
The storage format is used for storing EVRC-B-encoded speech frames, for example as a file or an e-mail attachment. The file begins with a magic number to identify the vocoder that is used. The magic number for EVRC-B corresponds to the ASCII character string #!EVRC-B\n, or 0x2321 0x4556 0x5243 0x2d42 0x0a in hexadecimal. The newline is an important part of both this magic number and the #!EVRC\n magic number defined in section 11 of RFC 3558, and it must be included in any comparison of either magic number, since otherwise a prefix of the EVRC-B magic number could be mistaken for the EVRC magic number.

The codec data frames are stored in consecutive order, with a single Table of Contents entry field, extended to one octet, prefixing each codec data frame. The Table of Contents field, as defined in section 5.1 of RFC 3558, is extended to one octet by setting the four most significant bits of the octet to zero, so a Table of Contents value of 4, a full-rate frame, is stored as 0x04. Speech frames lost in transmission and non-received frames must be stored as erasure frames, to maintain synchronization with the original media.
sections.plainLanguage: To store EVRC-B speech in a file, the file starts with a marker naming the codec, and each stored frame is prefixed with a one-octet index of its rate. Frames that never arrived are stored as erasure frames so the file stays in step with the original.

sections.title: Media Types and Their Parameters
sections.content:
The document registers six media types under the type name audio. The subtypes EVRC1, EVRCB, EVRCB0 and EVRCB1 are new, and the registrations of EVRC and EVRC0 from RFC 3558 are updated. None of them has a required parameter.

The optional parameters fall into groups. ptime and maxptime describe how much media a packet carries; the default maxptime is 200 milliseconds, and it should be a multiple of the 20 millisecond duration of one codec frame. fixedrate says which rate is used in single-rate operation, with 0.5 for the half rate and 1 for the full rate; if the parameter is absent, the half rate is assumed. maxinterleave caps the interleaving length used across the session, with a default of 5.

Four parameters exist for discontinuous transmission. silencesupp is 0 or 1 and states whether the sender is capable and willing to use silence suppression; if it is absent, the default value 1 must be assumed. dtxmax and dtxmin, both from 0 to 255, give the maximum and minimum interval in frames between the occasional updates the sender makes to the receiver during silence; the defaults are 32 and 12. hangover, from 0 to 255, is the number of consecutive silence frames sent at the end of an active speech interval before the discontinuous transmission interval begins, with a default of 1, and setting it to 1 or more is recommended because the presence of those frames helps the receiver identify the start of the silent period.
sections.plainLanguage: Each media type carries optional settings. Some say how much speech goes in a packet and which rate to use. Four more control silence suppression: whether to use it, how often to send a background-noise update during silence, and how many silent frames to send before going quiet.

sections.title: Negotiating the Parameters
sections.content:
All SDP parameters in this payload format are declarative, and all reasonable values are expected to be supported. In particular, when discontinuous transmission is supported, the RTP sender implementation should support the hangover, dtxmin and dtxmax values from 0 to 255, so the standard usage of Offer/Answer as described in RFC 3264 should be followed.

Three rules must be followed while negotiating the discontinuous transmission parameters. If any such parameter is not present in either the offer or the answer, the default value must be assumed. If silencesupp is present and set to 0 in either the offer or the answer, the values of all received parameters other than silencesupp should be ignored. In an offer or an answer, the value of dtxmax should always be larger than or equal to the value of dtxmin, regardless of whether the values are indicated explicitly or implicitly by default; and if the indicated value of dtxmin is larger than that of dtxmax, the RTP sender must ignore the indicated values and must fall back on the default dtxmin and dtxmax values.

The mapping into SDP is direct. The MIME type goes in the media name, the subtype goes in the rtpmap encoding name, ptime and maxptime go in their own attributes, and maxinterleave, fixedrate, silencesupp, dtxmax, dtxmin and hangover are copied into the format attribute as name and value pairs.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends agree these settings the usual way, by offering and answering. If a setting is missing, the default applies. If either side says no to silence suppression, the other settings are ignored. And the maximum interval must never be smaller than the minimum interval.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Implementations using the payload defined in this specification are subject to the security considerations discussed in RFC 3558, RFC 3550, and any appropriate profile such as RFC 3551. The payload does not specify any different security services.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is added here. The usual security rules for RTP payloads apply, and this payload does not change them.

viz.caption: THE COMPACT BUNDLED PACKET FROM RFC 4788 SECTION 4
THE FOUR PARAMETERS THAT CONTROL SILENCE SUPPRESSION

items.title: silencesupp
items.text: 0 or 1. Says the sender is capable and willing to use silence suppression. Absent means 1.

items.title: dtxmax
items.text: 0 to 255 frames. The longest gap the receiver expects between background-noise updates. The default is 32.

items.title: dtxmin
items.text: 0 to 255 frames. The shortest gap the receiver expects between background-noise updates. The default is 12.

items.title: hangover
items.text: 0 to 255 frames. How many silent frames are sent at the end of speech before the silent period starts. The default is 1.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE SESSION DESCRIPTION FOR EVRC WITH SILENCE SUPPRESSION

data.title: SDP example
data.code:
m=audio 49120 RTP/AVP 97
a=rtpmap:97 EVRC/8000
a=fmtp:97 silencesupp=1 dtxmax=32 dtxmin=12 hangover=1
